## Impact
Users can queue a withdrawal and potentially withdraw completely if ```PAUSED_EIGENPODS_VERIFY_OVERCOMMITTED = false```
## Proof of Concept
We need to look at two functions. The first one is 
```solidity
function verifyOvercommittedStake(
    uint40 validatorIndex,
    BeaconChainProofs.ValidatorFieldsAndBalanceProofs calldata proofs,
    bytes32[] calldata validatorFields,
    uint256 beaconChainETHStrategyIndex,
    uint64 oracleBlockNumber
) external onlyWhenNotPaused(PAUSED_EIGENPODS_VERIFY_OVERCOMMITTED) {
```

```solidity
function queueWithdrawal(
    uint256[] calldata strategyIndexes,
    IStrategy[] calldata strategies,
    uint256[] calldata shares,
    address withdrawer,
    bool undelegateIfPossible
)
    external
    onlyWhenNotPaused(PAUSED_WITHDRAWALS)
    onlyNotFrozen(msg.sender)
    nonReentrant
    returns (bytes32)
{
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The Merkle library's staticcall function contains a vulnerability that could lead to the failure of the entire operation if the invoked external contract exceeds the provided 2300 gas stipend. An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to launch a Denial of Service (DoS) attack on the contract. They could achieve this by creating and deploying a sophisticated contract that surpasses the stipulated gas allowance, thereby causing the contract to become unresponsive or frozen, leading to loss of data or funds.

The weakness within the given code is related to the utilization of the staticcall function in the processInclusionProofSha256 function. More precisely, the staticcall function is employed to execute an external contract and obtain the calculated hash of the sibling node. However, the staticcall function has a restricted gas allowance of 2300, which is inadequate for executing most contracts. Thus, if the external contract is intricate and requires more gas, the function will fail and result in the failure of the entire operation.

This vulnerability could be exploited by an attacker who creates a contract that requires more gas than the staticcall stipend and supplies its address as an argument to the processInclusionProofSha256 function. When the staticcall function is executed, it will fail, resulting in the failure of the entire operation. The attacker can repeat the processInclusionProofSha256 function, supplying different contract addresses each time, until they find a contract that doesn't require more gas than the stipend.
